I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030.

This is Real Hope, Real Change. Faster action on transport is vital for cleaner air, lower household bills, and a safer climate for young people. Electric vehicles are now cheaper to run, and when powered by publicly owned renewable energy they cut emissions and keep money in our communities — not in the pockets of fossil fuel shareholders. But a transition must be fair: the government should fund a nationwide insulation and charging programme, retrofit grants for low-income households, and scrappage schemes so renters, low-earners and public sector workers aren’t left behind. Free or reduced fares for young people and investment in local buses, trains and active travel will make car-free life possible, not just desirable.

This ban is about the common good — protecting children’s health with clean air outside schools, creating green jobs, and using a wealth tax to pay for it. For the Common Good: phase out petrol cars by 2030 and build Fairer, Greener Communities.

Ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030? I oppose it — strongly. This is another Westminster diktat from the Green Blob, handed down by people who’ve never filled a tractor with diesel or struggled to get to work when the bus doesn’t run. For ordinary folk a petrol ban means forced expense, scrapped livelihoods and fewer choices. Electric cars are fine for some, but not everyone can afford them, charge them where they live, or rely on them for long rural journeys and farm work.

Pushing through this ban by 2030 will hit working families, haulage firms, farmers and small businesses hardest — the very backbone of Britain. It’s ideologically-driven policy dressed up as climate virtue-signalling, and it leaves households with higher bills and hidden taxes to pay for charging networks and subsidies. Instead of top-down bans, let’s invest in British energy, stop green levies on bills, and focus on practical solutions that don’t punish drivers. Scrap the 2030 petrol car ban — restore common-sense freedom and protect livelihoods.

I strongly oppose the plan to ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. This is another Westminster edict from the Green Blob — an ideological crusade that will hit ordinary people hardest. Working families, tradespeople, and farmers rely on petrol vehicles to get the job done. Forcing a rapid switch to electric cars will push up costs, wreck rural life where chargers are scarce, and strand those who can’t afford pricey new models.

This isn’t about cleaner air for the nation; it’s about imposing elite preferences on hard-working Brits. Charging infrastructure is patchy, batteries degrade, and the electricity price hikes from green levies mean running an EV won’t be cheap. Small businesses and van drivers will face crippling replacement bills. Instead of punishing drivers, government should focus on affordable, practical energy and improved transport choices — not draconian bans dreamed up in Whitehall.

Scrap the 2030 petrol ban. Stop the War on Drivers. Protect jobs, rural communities, and household budgets — put common sense before costly climate dogma.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. Real Hope, Real Change means protecting our future and our pockets — and this is a policy that does both. Electric vehicles are now cheaper to run, and when paired with a rapid roll-out of public charging, better public transport and expanded bike lanes, a 2030 ban drives down household bills, cuts toxic air in our communities, and slashes the emissions warming our planet.

But this must be done fairly. We should fund grants and low-interest loans to help low-income families and small businesses replace vehicles, invest in insulating homes so people can afford cleaner energy, and bring charging infrastructure into every town. Profits from publicly owned energy networks should be reinvested to support this transition, not siphoned off to shareholders.

A 2030 ban is about more than cars — it’s about a safer, healthier future, thriving local high streets, and public transport that works for everyone. For the Common Good, let’s choose a Fairer, Greener Britain.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by no later than 2030. This is Real Hope, Real Change — a bold, practical step that protects people and planet. Petrol cars lock us into rising bills, polluted streets and the climate chaos that steals young people's futures. A 2030 deadline gives industry, workers and communities time to adapt while sending a clear signal that the fossil-fuel era is over.

But a ban without support would be unfair. For the common good, it must be paired with public investment: free or cheap electric buses and trains, grants and zero-interest loans for people to switch to electric vehicles when needed, and large-scale home and workplace charging rolled out by public utilities. We must retrain and back workers in car manufacturing and garages for the green transition. Wealthy corporations must pay their fair share to fund it.

Fairer, Greener Communities means cleaner air, cheaper running costs, and a secure future for everyone. I back a 2030 petrol-car sales ban — if it comes with a just, publicly funded transition.

Ban the sale of new petrol cars by 2030? Absolutely not. This is the Westminster elite pushing yet another expensive, dogmatic plan while ordinary people pay the price. Working families, rural communities and small businesses rely on reliable petrol cars — not fragile, costly electric alternatives forced on them by out-of-touch politicians and the so-called “green” lobby.

Scrapping petrol sales by 2030 would spike costs for households already crushed by soaring energy and living bills. It’s a regressive tax on drivers: tradespeople, farmers, and shift workers who need robust vehicles, not tinny city toys that can’t cope on muddy lanes or long shifts without hours of charging. It will hammer the North, where driving is a necessity, and hand more power to foreign supply chains and expensive green technology firms.

We should reject ideological deadlines and instead focus on practical solutions: boost domestic energy production, ditch green levies, and let people choose. Scrap Net Zero targets that drive up costs. Stop the war on drivers — keep Britain moving, keep people in work, and restore common-sense freedom.

I strongly support a government ban on the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. This is a practical, fair step that tackles the climate emergency and the cost-of-living squeeze at the same time. Petrol cars lock families into rising fuel bills and pollution; accelerating the shift to electric and zero-emission vehicles will cut household running costs, clean up the air around schools and hospitals, and cut our dependence on volatile fossil-fuel markets controlled by profit-driven corporations.

But a ban without support would be unfair. We must pair it with publicly owned charging infrastructure, grants and low-cost loans for people on low incomes, and a nationwide home-insulation and retrofit programme so electric vehicles and cleaner transport are truly affordable. We should prioritise buses, cycling and walking in towns so people can choose cheaper alternatives to car use. With a wealth tax to fund the transition and public ownership of key energy systems, this policy becomes a chance for real hope, real change — Fairer, Greener Communities and a secure future for everyone.
